mcq.q: A sum of ₹1,82,500 amounts to ₹3,57,700 in 8 years at simple interest. The rate of interest per annum is:
mcq.explain: Interest = amount − principal = 3,57,700 − 1,82,500 = ₹1,75,200. Simple interest I = P × R × T / 100, so R = 100 × I / (P × T) = 100 × 1,75,200 / (1,82,500 × 8) = 12%. Dividing by the amount instead of the principal gives a lower, wrong rate.
mcq.fast: Interest per year = ₹21,900; as a % of ₹1,82,500 that is 12%.

mcq.q: A sum of ₹1,10,000 amounts to ₹1,16,600 in 3 years at simple interest. The rate of interest per annum is:
mcq.explain: Interest = amount − principal = 1,16,600 − 1,10,000 = ₹6,600. Simple interest I = P × R × T / 100, so R = 100 × I / (P × T) = 100 × 6,600 / (1,10,000 × 3) = 2%. Dividing by the amount instead of the principal gives a lower, wrong rate.
mcq.fast: Interest per year = ₹2,200; as a % of ₹1,10,000 that is 2%.

mcq.q: ₹40,000 is lent in two parts, one at 12% and the other at 15% simple interest per annum. The total interest for one year is ₹5,370. The part lent at 12% is:
mcq.fast: Alligation: if all were at 15% interest = ₹6,000; each rupee moved to 12% cuts 3 paise. Shortfall ₹630 ÷ 0.03 = ₹21,000.

mcq.q: ₹70,000 is lent in two parts, one at 12% and the other at 15% simple interest per annum. The total interest for one year is ₹8,760. The part lent at 12% is:
mcq.fast: Alligation: if all were at 15% interest = ₹10,500; each rupee moved to 12% cuts 3 paise. Shortfall ₹1,740 ÷ 0.03 = ₹58,000.

mcq.q: The compound interest on ₹2,15,000 for 2 years at 8% per annum, compounded half-yearly, is:
mcq.explain: Compounded half-yearly: rate per period i = 8% ÷ 2 = 4% and periods n = 2 × 2 = 4. Amount = 2,15,000 × (1 + 0.04)^4 = ₹2,51,519.59. CI = amount − principal = ₹36,519.59. Using 8% with annual periods ignores the more frequent compounding.
mcq.fast: Calculator: type 1.04, press × once, then = 3 times to get (1.04)^4; then × 2,15,000 and subtract 2,15,000.

mcq.q: The compound interest on ₹1,00,000 for 1 year at 16% per annum, compounded quarterly, is:
mcq.explain: Compounded quarterly: rate per period i = 16% ÷ 4 = 4% and periods n = 1 × 4 = 4. Amount = 1,00,000 × (1 + 0.04)^4 = ₹1,16,985.86. CI = amount − principal = ₹16,985.86. Using 16% with annual periods ignores the more frequent compounding.
mcq.fast: Calculator: type 1.04, press × once, then = 3 times to get (1.04)^4; then × 1,00,000 and subtract 1,00,000.

mcq.q: At 15% per annum, the 2-year compound interest on a certain sum exceeds the 2-year simple interest on it by ₹3,825. The sum is:
mcq.explain: For 2 years, CI − SI = P × (R/100)², because the only extra is the interest earned in year 2 on year-1 interest. So 3,825 = P × (15/100)² = P × 0.0225, giving P = ₹1,70,000. Using P × R/100 only (₹25,500) is the common slip.

mcq.q: At 8% per annum, the 2-year compound interest on a certain sum exceeds the 2-year simple interest on it by ₹880. The sum is:
mcq.explain: For 2 years, CI − SI = P × (R/100)², because the only extra is the interest earned in year 2 on year-1 interest. So 880 = P × (8/100)² = P × 0.0064, giving P = ₹1,37,500. Using P × R/100 only (₹11,000) is the common slip.

mcq.q: The effective annual rate of interest equivalent to a nominal rate of 15% per annum compounded quarterly is:
mcq.explain: Effective rate E = (1 + i)^m − 1, where i = 15%/4 = 3.75% per period and m = 4. E = (1 + 0.0375)^4 − 1 = 0.1587, i.e. 15.87%. It is always above the nominal rate when interest is compounded more than once a year.
mcq.fast: Calculator: type 1.0375, press × once, then = 3 times to get (1.0375)^4; subtract 1. Answer must be a little above 15%.

mcq.q: The effective annual rate of interest equivalent to a nominal rate of 7% per annum compounded quarterly is:
mcq.explain: Effective rate E = (1 + i)^m − 1, where i = 7%/4 = 1.75% per period and m = 4. E = (1 + 0.0175)^4 − 1 = 0.0719, i.e. 7.19%. It is always above the nominal rate when interest is compounded more than once a year.
mcq.fast: Calculator: type 1.0175, press × once, then = 3 times to get (1.0175)^4; subtract 1. Answer must be a little above 7%.

mcq.q: A deposit earns a nominal 8% per annum while inflation is 4% per annum. The real rate of interest (exact formula) is about:
mcq.explain: Real rate = (1 + nominal)/(1 + inflation) − 1 = 1.08/1.04 − 1 = 0.0385, i.e. about 3.85%. The quick estimate 8 − 4 = 4% slightly overstates the real return because it ignores that inflation also erodes the interest.
mcq.fast: Divide: 1.08 ÷ 1.04 − 1; the answer is a little below 4%.

mcq.q: A deposit earns a nominal 15% per annum while inflation is 4% per annum. The real rate of interest (exact formula) is about:
mcq.explain: Real rate = (1 + nominal)/(1 + inflation) − 1 = 1.15/1.04 − 1 = 0.1058, i.e. about 10.58%. The quick estimate 15 − 4 = 11% slightly overstates the real return because it ignores that inflation also erodes the interest.
mcq.fast: Divide: 1.15 ÷ 1.04 − 1; the answer is a little below 11%.

mcq.q: ₹29,000 is deposited at the end of every year for 4 years at 12% per annum compound interest. The amount at the end of 4 years is:
mcq.explain: This is the future value of an annuity regular: FV = A × [(1 + i)^n − 1]/i = 29,000 × [(1.12)^4 − 1]/0.12 = ₹1,38,600.51. The last deposit earns no interest. If deposits were at the beginning of each year (annuity due), multiply by 1.12, giving the trap ₹1,55,232.57.
mcq.topic: Annuities — regular and due; future value; sinking fund

mcq.q: ₹45,000 is deposited at the end of every year for 4 years at 7% per annum compound interest. The amount at the end of 4 years is:
mcq.explain: This is the future value of an annuity regular: FV = A × [(1 + i)^n − 1]/i = 45,000 × [(1.07)^4 − 1]/0.07 = ₹1,99,797.44. The last deposit earns no interest. If deposits were at the beginning of each year (annuity due), multiply by 1.07, giving the trap ₹2,13,783.26.
mcq.topic: Annuities — regular and due; future value; sinking fund

mcq.q: A scholarship pays ₹1,20,000 at the BEGINNING of each year for 9 years. At 8% per annum, its present value is:
mcq.explain: Payments at the beginning of each period form an annuity due. PV = A × [1 − (1 + i)^−n]/i × (1 + i) = 1,20,000 × 6.2469 × 1.08 = ₹8,09,596.67. Equivalently, the first payment is received today and the other 8 form an annuity regular.
mcq.topic: Annuities — regular and due; future value; sinking fund
mcq.fast: PV due = PV regular × 1.08; or A + A × P(8, 8%).

mcq.q: A scholarship pays ₹5,000 at the BEGINNING of each year for 3 years. At 12% per annum, its present value is:
mcq.explain: Payments at the beginning of each period form an annuity due. PV = A × [1 − (1 + i)^−n]/i × (1 + i) = 5,000 × 2.4018 × 1.12 = ₹13,450.26. Equivalently, the first payment is received today and the other 2 form an annuity regular.
mcq.topic: Annuities — regular and due; future value; sinking fund
mcq.fast: PV due = PV regular × 1.12; or A + A × P(2, 12%).

mcq.q: A company must replace a machine costing ₹10,50,000 after 11 years. How much must it set aside at the end of each year in a sinking fund earning 5% per annum?
mcq.explain: The deposits are an annuity regular whose future value must equal ₹10,50,000: A × [(1 + i)^n − 1]/i = 10,50,000. So A = 10,50,000 × 0.05/[(1.05)^11 − 1] = ₹73,908.34. Dividing ₹10,50,000 by 11 ignores the interest the fund earns.
mcq.topic: Annuities — regular and due; future value; sinking fund

mcq.q: A company must replace a machine costing ₹43,00,000 after 12 years. How much must it set aside at the end of each year in a sinking fund earning 6% per annum?
mcq.explain: The deposits are an annuity regular whose future value must equal ₹43,00,000: A × [(1 + i)^n − 1]/i = 43,00,000. So A = 43,00,000 × 0.06/[(1.06)^12 − 1] = ₹2,54,891.23. Dividing ₹43,00,000 by 12 ignores the interest the fund earns.
mcq.topic: Annuities — regular and due; future value; sinking fund

mcq.q: Find the present value of ₹36,000 received at the end of each year for 15 years if money is worth 10% per annum.
mcq.explain: PV of an annuity regular = A × [1 − (1 + i)^−n]/i = 36,000 × [1 − (1.10)^−15]/0.1 = ₹2,73,818.86. The present value is always less than the total paid (36,000 × 15 = ₹5,40,000) because later rupees are worth less today.
mcq.topic: Present value of annuities; loan amortisation (EMI)

mcq.q: Find the present value of ₹97,500 received at the end of each year for 8 years if money is worth 10% per annum.
mcq.explain: PV of an annuity regular = A × [1 − (1 + i)^−n]/i = 97,500 × [1 − (1.10)^−8]/0.1 = ₹5,20,155.30. The present value is always less than the total paid (97,500 × 8 = ₹7,80,000) because later rupees are worth less today.
mcq.topic: Present value of annuities; loan amortisation (EMI)

mcq.q: A loan of ₹13,00,000 at 8% per annum is to be repaid in equal annual instalments over 5 years (interest compounded annually). The instalment (EMI) is:
mcq.explain: The loan equals the present value of the instalments: L = E × [1 − (1 + i)^−n]/i, with i = 8% per period and n = 5. So E = 13,00,000 × 0.08/[1 − (1 + 0.08)^−5] = ₹3,25,593.39. Spreading flat interest (₹3,64,000.00) overstates the cost.
mcq.topic: Present value of annuities; loan amortisation (EMI)
mcq.fast: EMI = L × i/(1 − (1 + i)^−n): compute (1 + i)^n with repeated ×, take its reciprocal, subtract from 1.

mcq.q: A loan of ₹13,50,000 at 8% per annum is to be repaid in equal monthly instalments over 4 years (interest compounded monthly). The instalment (EMI) is:
mcq.explain: The loan equals the present value of the instalments: L = E × [1 − (1 + i)^−n]/i, with i = 0.6667% per period and n = 48. So E = 13,50,000 × 0.006667/[1 − (1 + 0.006667)^−48] = ₹32,957.45. Spreading flat interest (₹37,125.00) overstates the cost.
mcq.topic: Present value of annuities; loan amortisation (EMI)
mcq.fast: EMI = L × i/(1 − (1 + i)^−n): compute (1 + i)^n with repeated ×, take its reciprocal, subtract from 1.

mcq.q: A firm leases out an asset costing ₹16,00,000 for 7 years with no salvage value. To earn 12% per annum, the annual lease rent (paid at year end) should be:
mcq.explain: The lessor wants the present value of the 7 rents at 12% to equal the cost: Rent × P(7, 12%) = 16,00,000. P(7, 12%) = [1 − (1.12)^−7]/0.12 = 4.5638, so Rent = ₹3,50,588.38. Cost ÷ years recovers the cost but no return.
mcq.topic: Applications: leasing, capital expenditure, bond valuation
mcq.fast: Rent = cost ÷ P(7, 12%) — the same calculation as an EMI.

mcq.q: A firm leases out an asset costing ₹20,00,000 for 4 years with no salvage value. To earn 15% per annum, the annual lease rent (paid at year end) should be:
mcq.explain: The lessor wants the present value of the 4 rents at 15% to equal the cost: Rent × P(4, 15%) = 20,00,000. P(4, 15%) = [1 − (1.15)^−4]/0.15 = 2.8550, so Rent = ₹7,00,530.70. Cost ÷ years recovers the cost but no return.
mcq.topic: Applications: leasing, capital expenditure, bond valuation
mcq.fast: Rent = cost ÷ P(4, 15%) — the same calculation as an EMI.

mcq.q: A bond of face value ₹10,000 pays a 6% annual coupon and is redeemed at par after 6 years. If the required yield is 8% per annum, its value is:
mcq.explain: Value = PV of coupons + PV of redemption = 600 × P(6, 8%) + 10,000 × (1.08)^−6 = 2,773.73 + 6,301.70 = ₹9,075.42. When the coupon rate is below the yield, the bond sells at a discount to face value.
mcq.topic: Applications: leasing, capital expenditure, bond valuation
mcq.fast: Sanity check first: coupon 6% < yield 8% ⇒ price < ₹10,000; then discount the coupons and the redemption.

mcq.q: A bond of face value ₹10,000 pays a 7% annual coupon and is redeemed at par after 4 years. If the required yield is 11% per annum, its value is:
mcq.explain: Value = PV of coupons + PV of redemption = 700 × P(4, 11%) + 10,000 × (1.11)^−4 = 2,171.71 + 6,587.31 = ₹8,759.02. When the coupon rate is below the yield, the bond sells at a discount to face value.
mcq.topic: Applications: leasing, capital expenditure, bond valuation
mcq.fast: Sanity check first: coupon 7% < yield 11% ⇒ price < ₹10,000; then discount the coupons and the redemption.

mcq.q: What should you pay today for a stream that pays ₹65,500 at the end of the first year and then grows at 4% a year forever, when money is worth 10% a year?
mcq.explain: This is a growing perpetuity: PV = first payment ÷ (r − g) = 65,500 ÷ (10% − 4%) = 65,500 ÷ 0.06 = ₹10,91,666.67. Growth makes it worth more than the level perpetuity (₹6,55,000.00). The formula needs r > g.
mcq.fast: Divide the first payment by (r − g) = 6%: 65,500 × 100/6.

mcq.q: What should you pay today for a stream that pays ₹97,000 at the end of the first year and then grows at 4% a year forever, when money is worth 6% a year?
mcq.explain: This is a growing perpetuity: PV = first payment ÷ (r − g) = 97,000 ÷ (6% − 4%) = 97,000 ÷ 0.02 = ₹48,50,000.00. Growth makes it worth more than the level perpetuity (₹16,16,666.67). The formula needs r > g.
mcq.fast: Divide the first payment by (r − g) = 2%: 97,000 × 100/2.

mcq.q: What should you pay today for a stream that pays ₹90,500 at the end of the first year and then grows at 4% a year forever, when money is worth 5% a year?
mcq.explain: This is a growing perpetuity: PV = first payment ÷ (r − g) = 90,500 ÷ (5% − 4%) = 90,500 ÷ 0.01 = ₹90,50,000.00. Growth makes it worth more than the level perpetuity (₹18,10,000.00). The formula needs r > g.
mcq.fast: Divide the first payment by (r − g) = 1%: 90,500 × 100/1.

mcq.q: A project costs ₹8,50,000 now and returns ₹3,16,000, ₹2,73,000, ₹2,67,000, ₹3,22,000 at the end of years 1 to 4. At a cost of capital of 8%, its NPV is:
mcq.explain: NPV = Σ CFₜ/(1 + k)ᵗ − initial outlay. Discount factors at 8%: 0.9259, 0.8573, 0.7938, 0.7350. PV of inflows = ₹9,75,278.91; NPV = ₹1,25,278.91. A positive NPV: accept. Not discounting at all gives ₹3,28,000.
mcq.fast: Multiply each flow by its discount factor (1 ÷ 1.k repeatedly on the calculator, using GT/M+ to add), then subtract the cost.

mcq.q: A project costs ₹2,00,000 now and returns ₹57,000, ₹65,000, ₹74,000, ₹62,000 at the end of years 1 to 4. At a cost of capital of 8%, its NPV is:
mcq.explain: NPV = Σ CFₜ/(1 + k)ᵗ − initial outlay. Discount factors at 8%: 0.9259, 0.8573, 0.7938, 0.7350. PV of inflows = ₹2,12,820.24; NPV = ₹12,820.24. A positive NPV: accept. Not discounting at all gives ₹58,000.
mcq.fast: Multiply each flow by its discount factor (1 ÷ 1.k repeatedly on the calculator, using GT/M+ to add), then subtract the cost.

mcq.q: An investment grew from ₹1,10,000 to ₹1,56,000 in 6 years. Its compound annual growth rate (CAGR) is about:
mcq.explain: CAGR = (ending ÷ beginning)^(1/n) − 1 = (1,56,000/1,10,000)^(1/6) − 1 = 1.4182^(1/6) − 1 ≈ 6%. The simple average 6.97% ignores compounding and overstates the yearly growth. CAGR is the steady yearly rate that would turn the starting value into the ending value.
mcq.topic: Compound annual growth rate (CAGR) and rate of return
mcq.fast: Back-substitute: (1 + option)^6 should give the growth multiple 1.4182. Rule of 72 gives a rough check.

mcq.q: An investment grew from ₹4,80,000 to ₹9,65,500 in 5 years. Its compound annual growth rate (CAGR) is about:
mcq.explain: CAGR = (ending ÷ beginning)^(1/n) − 1 = (9,65,500/4,80,000)^(1/5) − 1 = 2.0115^(1/5) − 1 ≈ 15%. The simple average 20.23% ignores compounding and overstates the yearly growth. CAGR is the steady yearly rate that would turn the starting value into the ending value.
mcq.topic: Compound annual growth rate (CAGR) and rate of return
mcq.fast: Back-substitute: (1 + option)^5 should give the growth multiple 2.0115. Rule of 72 gives a rough check.

mcq.q: A machine costs ₹15,00,000 and depreciates at 20% per annum on the reducing (written-down) balance. Its value after 2 years is:
mcq.explain: Reducing-balance depreciation is compound interest in reverse: value = C × (1 − r)^n = 15,00,000 × (1 − 0.2)^2 = 15,00,000 × 0.64 = ₹9,60,000.00. Straight-line thinking (deducting 20% of cost every year) gives a lower, wrong figure.
mcq.fast: Calculator: type 0.8, press × once, then = 1 times to get (0.8)^2; then × 15,00,000.

mcq.q: A machine costs ₹4,75,000 and depreciates at 12% per annum on the reducing (written-down) balance. Its value after 4 years is:
mcq.explain: Reducing-balance depreciation is compound interest in reverse: value = C × (1 − r)^n = 4,75,000 × (1 − 0.12)^4 = 4,75,000 × 0.599695 = ₹2,84,855.30. Straight-line thinking (deducting 12% of cost every year) gives a lower, wrong figure.
mcq.fast: Calculator: type 0.88, press × once, then = 3 times to get (0.88)^4; then × 4,75,000.

mcq.q: At 5% per annum compound interest (compounded annually), after how many complete years will a sum first become more than double itself?
mcq.explain: We need the smallest n with (1.05)^n > 2. (1.05)^14 = 1.9799 is still below 2, while (1.05)^15 = 2.0789 exceeds it. So 15 years. Simple interest would need 20 years — compounding is faster.
mcq.fast: Rule of 72: about 14.4 years; confirm with (1.05)^n on the calculator.

mcq.q: At 11% per annum compound interest (compounded annually), after how many complete years will a sum first become more than double itself?
mcq.explain: We need the smallest n with (1.11)^n > 2. (1.11)^6 = 1.8704 is still below 2, while (1.11)^7 = 2.0762 exceeds it. So 7 years. Simple interest would need 9.09 years — compounding is faster.
mcq.fast: Rule of 72: about 6.5 years; confirm with (1.11)^n on the calculator.
